quoted_clause: the gate closes only when the host class is replicated to ~5 hosts (Chs. 15–17)
observed: The same candidate paragraph says a lone host cannot carry the arrival rate: '~6 hosts are needed for the canonical average, and ~21 at peak'. Table 12-1 then says candidate (a) 'needs ~5 hosts'. These are different denominators: ~5 is the average prefill-compute screen (92K ÷ 19.8K ≈ 4.65), while ~6 is the average KV/service-time screen (10 × 8.6 ÷ 17 ≈ 5.06 → 6) and ~21 is the peak KV/service-time screen (40 × 8.6 ÷ 17 ≈ 20.2 → 21).
evidence: Recomputation from the book's own inputs: 92,000 input tok/s ÷ 19,800 prefill tok/s ≈ 4.65 prefill hosts at average load; 10 rps × 8.6 s ÷ 17 slots ≈ 5.06 → 6 KV-slot hosts at average load; 40 rps × 8.6 s ÷ 17 slots ≈ 20.2 → 21 KV-slot hosts at peak. The ~5-host figure therefore does not close the throughput/capacity gate at the canonical peak and is not interchangeable with the ~6/~21 figures.
root_cause: Conflating the prefill-compute ceiling with the KV/service-time capacity screen and omitting the peak-load denominator in the candidate verdict.
correction: State the three screens separately: ~5 hosts for average prefill compute, ~6 hosts for average KV-slot capacity, and ~21 hosts for peak KV-slot capacity. Candidate (a)'s single-host throughput gate is not closed by ~5 hosts; the peak fleet remains ~21 hosts before headroom.
acceptance_test: Recompute and display all three host counts from their stated denominators in Ch. 12 §3, Table 12-1, and Table 12-2; verify that no sentence uses ~5 hosts to claim the canonical peak throughput gate is closed.

quoted_clause: but neither quality nor throughput makes it competitive for this workload
observed: The same section says 'Throughput is genuinely much higher on the smaller model' and computes ~24,700 prefill tokens/s on one H100 for the 7B candidate, versus ~2,471 per GPU for the 70B. Table 12-2 then shows candidate (c) needing only ~4 average / ~15 peak single-H100 cards, far fewer than the 70B candidates' ~5/~19 8×H100 hosts. The later mini-case also says candidate (c) 'faces the same throughput demand at peak, making it provisionally non-viable', which contradicts its own favorable throughput arithmetic.
evidence: 92,000 ÷ 24,725 ≈ 3.72 → ~4 cards average; 368,000 ÷ 24,725 ≈ 14.88 → ~15 cards peak. The open gate for candidate (c) is quality, not throughput. The phrase 'neither quality nor throughput' incorrectly adds throughput to the failure set.
root_cause: Conflating the quality gate with throughput viability; the smaller model's throughput advantage is acknowledged but then rhetorically discarded.
correction: Say candidate (c) is provisionally non-viable because its quality gate is open, while its illustrative throughput screen is favorable (~4 average / ~15 peak single-H100 cards). Do not claim it fails on throughput unless a measured throughput or SLO result is supplied.
acceptance_test: Revise Candidate (c), Table 12-1, Table 12-2, and §8 so that the verdict consistently says 'quality gate open; throughput screen favorable but unmeasured' and no sentence says throughput makes it non-competitive.

quoted_clause: model capability is the goal (Ch4's Quality dimension), never the bottleneck
observed: The chapter's own two-stage model and Ch. 12's candidate (c) treat quality/capability as a gate that can fail and eliminate a candidate. Ch. 14 §3 also gives candidate B failing the retrieval-QA quality threshold. Capability is therefore not 'never the bottleneck'; it can be the binding constraint when the quality threshold is unmet.
evidence: Ch. 12 §3 candidate (c): 'quality gate open (Ch 14)'; Ch. 14 §3: candidate B 'fails the retrieval-QA quality threshold' and 'B does not' qualify. These are explicit counterexamples to the universal 'never the bottleneck'.
root_cause: Overstatement of the distinction between capability screening and deployment selection; the sentence collapses 'not a serving-performance predictor' into 'never a bottleneck'.
correction: Replace with: capability is a screening gate and can be the binding constraint when the quality threshold is unmet; it is not a predictor of serving throughput or latency.
acceptance_test: Search Ch. 14 for 'never the bottleneck' and verify the revised sentence is consistent with the quality-gate failures in Ch. 12 and Ch. 14 §3.

quoted_clause: There is also an inference-specific family — context/pipeline partitioning, expert parallelism, and P/D disaggregation — which has no training analogue.
observed: The same section later says expert parallelism is '(Used in both training and inference for MoE models.)' and pipeline parallelism is defined as a training strategy with forward/backward activations and bubbles. Only P/D disaggregation is correctly described as serving-only with no training counterpart.
evidence: Ch. 10 §1 item 2 defines pipeline parallelism with 'activations flow forward, gradients flow backward'; item 4 says EP is used in both training and inference; item 6 says P/D disaggregation 'has no training counterpart'. The quoted sentence therefore contradicts the chapter's own strategy list.
root_cause: Overgeneralizing the serving-only family to include EP and pipeline/context partitioning, which have training analogues.
correction: Limit the 'no training analogue' claim to P/D disaggregation. State that EP and pipeline/context partitioning have training analogues or are used in both modes.
acceptance_test: Revise the sentence and verify that every strategy labeled 'inference-specific' or 'no training analogue' is consistent with the detailed definitions and the EP note in the same section.

observed: The chapter later states, and Ch. 11 establishes, that prefill is compute-bound and decode is bandwidth-bound. Labeling memory bandwidth as the resource for prefill throughput swaps the two regimes.
evidence: Ch. 11 §3: 'prefill is compute-bound ... decode is bandwidth-bound'. Ch. 12 §3 Candidate (a): 'prefill is compute-bound at this operating point'. The mental-model list should therefore read compute (prefill throughput) and memory bandwidth (decode throughput).
root_cause: Resource-label swap in the mental model.
correction: Change 'memory bandwidth (prefill throughput)' to 'compute (prefill throughput)' and, if decode is listed, 'memory bandwidth (decode throughput)'.
acceptance_test: Check Ch. 12 §2 against Ch. 11 §3 and Ch. 12 §3; verify no sentence assigns prefill throughput to memory bandwidth.

quoted_clause: every request re-runs the ~1.29 PFLOP prefill for those 8K tokens
observed: For a 70B model, 8K tokens of prefill is approximately 2 × 70×10^9 × 8,192 ≈ 1.15 PFLOP, not ~1.29 PFLOP. The ~1.29 PFLOP figure corresponds to the full ~9.2K canonical input (2 × 70×10^9 × 9,200 ≈ 1.29 PFLOP), not the 8K retrieved-context subset.
evidence: 2 × 70e9 × 8192 = 1.14688e15 FLOP ≈ 1.15 PFLOP. 2 × 70e9 × 9200 = 1.288e15 FLOP ≈ 1.29 PFLOP. The quoted clause attaches the 9.2K-token figure to the 8K-token population.
root_cause: Reusing the full 9.2K canonical prefill FLOP count for the 8K retrieved-context subset.
correction: Either say '~1.15 PFLOP for those 8K tokens' or say '~1.29 PFLOP for the full ~9.2K input'. Keep the token population explicit.
acceptance_test: Recompute the prefill FLOPs from 2 × parameter count × token count for both the 8K subset and the 9.2K full input; verify the quoted sentence uses the matching token count.

quoted_clause: Each pool therefore needs its own 8×H100 host (residency ~164 GB — weights plus one request's KV — comfortably under 640 GB).
observed: A serving pool must hold the in-flight KV for many concurrent requests, not one request's KV. At the canonical 40 rps peak and 8.6 s service time, Little's Law gives ~344 in-flight requests fleet-wide; even a single pool's share is far more than one request. The ~164 GB figure is weights plus one request's KV, not the pool's residency under load.
evidence: Ch. 11/Ch. 13 use 40 × 8.6 ≈ 344 in-flight requests at peak and ~24.1 GB KV per 9.2K request. One 8×H100 host has ~500 GB free after 140 GB weights, enough for roughly 20 such requests, not the full pool concurrency. The memory gate for candidate (b) must use the pool's concurrent KV population, not a single request.
root_cause: Denominator/population error: using one request's KV to pass a pool-level memory gate.
correction: State that ~164 GB is weights plus one request's KV only; the pool memory gate must include the measured or planned concurrent KV population. At peak, candidate (b)'s prefill and decode pools each require enough hosts to hold their in-flight KV, not one host per pool.
acceptance_test: Recompute candidate (b)'s memory gate using the peak in-flight request population per pool and the per-request KV footprint; verify the text no longer uses 'one request's KV' to conclude a pool fits one host.

quoted_clause: a single all-reduce never saturates the full link because the traffic is split across multiple GPUs and multiple links
observed: The universal 'never' is false at the boundary. A two-rank all-reduce over a single PCIe or NVLink path can saturate that link; whether traffic is split across multiple links depends on topology, rank placement, and the collective algorithm. The chapter's own ring model uses one directional link per rank and can be bandwidth-bound.
evidence: Counterexample: two ranks exchanging a large tensor over one NVLink/PCIe path have no 'multiple links' over which to split the all-reduce traffic; the collective can saturate the available directional bandwidth. The book's own ring arithmetic (245 GB per rank at 450 GB/s) is a bandwidth-bound model, not a guarantee that the link is never saturated.
root_cause: Universal claim about link utilization without a topology or rank-placement condition.
correction: Replace 'never saturates' with 'may not saturate a given link when the collective is striped across multiple links; on a single-path two-rank exchange it can be bandwidth-bound. Measure the deployed topology.'
acceptance_test: Construct a two-rank large-buffer all-reduce on a single link and measure link utilization; verify the revised sentence no longer makes an unconditional 'never' claim.

quoted_clause: Screening with deployment metrics — e.g. benchmarking a model's MMLU to pick a serving stack.
observed: MMLU is a capability benchmark, not a deployment metric. The bullet labels the error as 'screening with deployment metrics' but the example is capability screening used to pick a serving stack. The second bullet correctly describes 'selecting with leaderboards'.
evidence: Ch. 14 §1 defines MMLU as a capability benchmark and deployment benchmarks as TTFT/TPOT/goodput/KV utilization. The example in the first bullet is therefore mislabeled.
root_cause: Terminology swap in the mental-model error list.
correction: Change the first bullet to 'Screening with capability metrics to pick a serving stack — e.g. benchmarking a model's MMLU to choose a serving stack. (Wrong tool.)'
acceptance_test: Verify the first bullet uses 'capability' for MMLU and the second bullet uses 'leaderboard' for selection; no bullet calls MMLU a deployment metric.
